section_title: How will the gospel move forward through opposition?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 9 So be on your guard. You will be delivered over to the councils and beaten in the synagogues. On My account you will stand before governors and kings as witnesses to them. 10 And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations. 11 But when they arrest you and hand you over, do not worry beforehand what to say. Instead, speak whatever you are given at that time, for it will not be you speaking, but the Holy Spirit.

12 Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child. Children will rise against their parents and have them put to death. 13 You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.

context_lines: Jesus turns from public upheavals to the opposition His followers will face personally. Religious councils, beatings, governors, and kings will become part of their experience. Even family relationships may break under the pressure. He prepares them for costly loyalty rather than promising an easy mission.

Yet these threats do not stop the gospel. The hearings become opportunities to bear witness, and the Holy Spirit will supply what they need to say. This promise addresses their defense when arrested; it does not make study, preparation, or responsible teaching unnecessary. Acts later records Peter speaking before the authorities while filled with the Spirit, and apostles continuing to preach after being flogged. ([Acts 4:5–13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/4.htm); [Acts 5:40–42](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/5.htm))

The closing promise joins perseverance with being saved. The Greek verb σῴζω (sōzō, SOH-zoh) can describe rescue from danger or salvation through Christ. The word’s range alone cannot decide which is foremost here; the warning, the promised outcome, and the wider teaching must be considered together. ([Thayer, σῴζω](https://biblehub.com/greek/4982.htm))
common_interpretation_lines: Many Christians understand the closing promise as final salvation for those who remain faithful to Christ. They differ over how that continuing faith relates to God’s preserving grace. The Reformed position in Westminster says that those truly brought to Christ will finally persevere because God keeps them, even though they may fall into serious sin for a time. ([Westminster Confession 17](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html#Chapter_17))

The Catholic Church teaches that faith is God’s gift but can be lost, and calls believers to nourish it and persevere. Methodist teaching likewise says that people who have received grace can depart from it and, through God’s grace, repent and return. These readings treat continued faith as a real responsibility; they should not be reduced to the claim that people earn salvation by their own strength. ([Catechism 162](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_one/chapter_three/article_1/iii_the_characteristics_of_faith.html); [Methodist Articles VIII–XII](https://www.umc.org/en/content/articles-of-religion))

Another reading takes being saved here chiefly as physical rescue at Christ’s return for believers who survive the coming tribulation. Walvoord explains the matching promise in Matthew this way and distinguishes those survivors from believers who are killed yet still belong to Christ. This is that teacher’s explanation, not a position shared by all Protestants. ([Walvoord, Matthew 24:13](https://walvoord.com/article/218))
god_plan_lines: The warning includes a promise about God’s larger purpose: the gospel will be proclaimed to all nations. Opposition can become part of that advance. Paul describes his imprisonment as opening opportunities for the message and encouraging others to speak more boldly. The suffering is real, but it does not put God’s mission beyond reach. ([Philippians 1:12–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/philippians/1.htm))

Revelation shows the destination of that worldwide gathering: a vast people from every nation before God and the Lamb, brought through suffering and cared for by Him. Their hope rests in the Lamb’s saving work, and the One they follow becomes their shepherd. This supplies the wider hope behind costly witness without requiring a verdict here on every disputed stage of the timeline. ([Revelation 7:9–17](https://biblehub.com/bsb/revelation/7.htm))
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
